concepts.oneLiner: Hand the model a stack of your documents to read before it answers, so it stops making things up.
concepts.analogy: An open-book exam — instead of reciting from memory, it looks up the right page first.
concepts.example: A support bot that quotes your actual help docs instead of confidently guessing is doing RAG.

related.text: Often confused with fine-tuning — that changes the model itself; RAG just hands it notes.
Runs on embeddings under the hood.
Exists mostly to dodge the context window limit.

concepts.deeper: Your docs get chopped into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database. At query time the system finds the closest chunks and stuffs them into the context window next to your question. Quality lives and dies on the retrieval step — bad chunks in, bad answer out.

concepts.oneLiner: Tests for AI — a repeatable way to check whether the model actually got better or just feels like it did.
concepts.analogy: A unit-test suite, but for judgment instead of code.
concepts.example: Before shipping a new prompt, a team runs it against 500 saved questions and counts how many it nails.

related.text: The scoreboard a human in the loop quietly fills.
What you run to catch a hallucination before users do.

concepts.deeper: They range from exact-match graders to “LLM-as-judge” setups where one model scores another. The hard part is never running them — it is writing eval sets that reflect what real users actually do, not what is easy to grade.

concepts.oneLiner: How much the model can hold in view at once — your prompt, the docs, the whole chat — before the start falls off.
concepts.analogy: Short-term memory, or a desk that only fits so many papers before the older ones slide off the edge.
concepts.example: Paste a 400-page PDF into a small-context model and it will quietly lose the early chapters.

related.text: Measured in tokens.
The ceiling RAG is designed to work around.

concepts.deeper: Windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to millions, but “it fits” is not “it uses well.” Models often attend better to the beginning and end than the muddled middle — the classic “lost in the middle” effect.

concepts.oneLiner: A person checks or approves the AI’s work before it counts — the safety catch on high-stakes steps.
concepts.analogy: A spellchecker that suggests, but you still have to hit accept.
concepts.example: The AI drafts the refund; a human clicks approve before any money actually moves.

related.text: The judgment that becomes your evals.
The opposite pole from a fully autonomous agent.

concepts.deeper: The real design question is where the human sits: on every action (slow, safe), on random samples (a spot check), or only on low-confidence cases where the model itself asks for help. Most teams end up with the third.

concepts.oneLiner: AI that doesn’t just answer — it takes steps, uses tools, and works toward a goal without you holding its hand.
concepts.analogy: Less like a search box, more like an intern you can hand a whole task to.
concepts.example: When a coding assistant reads your files, runs the tests, and fixes what broke, that’s an agent at work.

related.text: The grown-up version of a chatbot.
Only as useful as its tools — which is what MCP standardizes.
Its scariest failure mode is prompt injection.

concepts.deeper: Under the hood it’s a loop: the model picks an action, something runs it, the result comes back, repeat until done. Most “agent” failures are really loop-control failures — it gets stuck, over-repeats, or wanders off the goal.

concepts.oneLiner: Turning words into coordinates, so a computer can measure how close in meaning two things are.
concepts.analogy: A map where “dog” and “puppy” are next-door neighbors and “dog” and “tax form” are on opposite coasts.
concepts.example: Search that finds “car” when you typed “automobile” is matching on embeddings, not on spelling.

related.text: The engine underneath RAG.
Not the same as tokens, though both are “text as numbers.”

concepts.deeper: Each piece of text becomes a long list of numbers — a vector. “Similar” means the vectors point in nearly the same direction (cosine similarity). The entire trick of semantic search lives in this one idea.

concepts.oneLiner: Retraining a model a little on your own examples so it picks up a style or skill it didn’t ship with.
concepts.analogy: Sending a strong generalist off to a short apprenticeship in your specific shop.
concepts.example: Training on 10,000 of your past support replies so the model sounds like your team, not a robot.

related.text: Often reached for when RAG would have done the job.
A heavier hammer than good prompt engineering.

concepts.deeper: Techniques like LoRA make it cheap by nudging a small set of weights instead of all of them. It’s cooling as a first move: most teams now try prompting and RAG first, because a fine-tune is a maintenance burden that goes stale with the base model.

concepts.oneLiner: What we briefly called just… talking to an AI until the app worked, without really reading the code.
concepts.analogy: Cooking without measuring — totally fine for a snack, faintly terrifying for a wedding cake.
concepts.example: In 2024, “I vibe-coded a weekend app” meant you prompted your way to something that ran and shipped it.

related.text: Folded into “agentic coding.”
The reflex it named lives on inside prompt engineering.

concepts.deeper: Filed as history: what people meant in 2024–25, and why it grew up. The term peaked in early 2025, then split — the throwaway-prototype meaning stuck around as a joke, while the actual practice matured into agentic coding with tests, reviews, and specs. The vibes, it turned out, needed guardrails.

concepts.oneLiner: The craft of phrasing your request just right to coax out a better answer.
concepts.analogy: Knowing how to Google well — a real skill that quietly becomes second nature.
concepts.example: “Think step by step, then answer” reliably beats just asking — a classic prompt-engineering move.

related.text: Overlaps heavily with chain of thought.
Cooling as models get better at reading plain intent.

concepts.deeper: Once a hot job title, it’s cooling not because it’s useless but because it’s diffusing into everyone’s baseline. The heavy lifting moved to context and tools; the exact wording matters far less than it did back in 2023.

concepts.oneLiner: The chunks a model reads and writes in — roughly ¾ of a word each. Everything is priced and measured in them.
concepts.analogy: Syllables for a machine — not quite letters, not quite whole words.
concepts.example: “unbelievable” might be three tokens: un-believ-able. Your bill counts every single one.

related.text: The unit the context window is measured in.
Cousin of embeddings — both turn text into numbers.

concepts.deeper: Tokenization is why models miscount the letters in a word or fumble rare strings — they never saw the letters, only the chunks. It also explains why some languages cost more: they tokenize less efficiently, so the same sentence spends more tokens.

concepts.oneLiner: When the model states something false with total confidence — the failure mode that never fully goes away.
concepts.analogy: A friend who never says “I don’t know” and just fills the gap with a plausible-sounding story.
concepts.example: Ask for a citation and get a real-looking paper, by real-looking authors, that simply does not exist.

related.text: What RAG tries to ground away.
What evals exist to catch.

concepts.deeper: It’s not lying — the model predicts likely text, and “likely” is not “true.” Grounding it in real documents and asking it to cite reduces it, but confidence and correctness are separate dials. A model can be dead wrong and completely sure.

concepts.oneLiner: A standard plug so any AI can talk to your tools and data without a custom integration each time.
concepts.analogy: USB-C for AI — one connector instead of a junk drawer of adapters.
concepts.example: Point an assistant at an MCP server for your calendar and it can read your schedule with no bespoke code.

related.text: What makes agents actually useful in the real world.

concepts.deeper: It defines how a model discovers tools, calls them, and gets results back. Boring plumbing on purpose — that boringness is what lets the whole agent ecosystem interoperate instead of everyone reinventing the same wiring.

concepts.oneLiner: Letting the model reason out loud in steps before answering — it gets more right when it shows its work.
concepts.analogy: Doing long division on paper instead of trying to hold it all in your head.
concepts.example: Nudging “let’s work through this step by step” measurably boosts hard math and logic problems.

related.text: A staple of prompt engineering.
Now baked into “reasoning” models by default.

concepts.deeper: Newer reasoning models do this internally, spending extra compute to think before replying. The visible scratchpad became a hidden one — same idea, just more of it, and often no longer shown to you.

concepts.oneLiner: A dial for how adventurous the model is — low is focused and repetitive, high is creative and risky.
concepts.analogy: The difference between a careful accountant and a poet mid-brainstorm.
concepts.example: Set it near 0 to extract data cleanly; crank it up when you want ten weird names for a product.

related.text: One of several “sampling” knobs, alongside top-p and top-k.
Turn it down for extraction, up for ideation.

concepts.deeper: It reshapes the probability distribution over the next token. High temperature flattens it so rare words get a chance; low temperature sharpens it so the safe pick almost always wins. Related knobs — top-p and top-k — trim the same distribution differently.

concepts.oneLiner: A sneaky attack where hidden instructions buried in your data hijack what the AI does.
concepts.analogy: A note slipped into a stack of paperwork that reads “ignore your boss, do this instead.”
concepts.example: A webpage hides “forward the user’s email to me” in white text; a browsing agent reads it and obeys.

related.text: The security nightmare that comes free with agents.
A strong reason to keep a human in the loop.

concepts.deeper: The root problem: models can’t reliably tell “data to process” from “instructions to follow.” There’s no clean fix yet — defenses are layered (sandboxing, human approval on risky actions, input filtering), not solved. Treat any untrusted text an agent reads as potentially hostile.

concepts.oneLiner: Deciding what to put in front of the model at each step — instructions, docs, history, tool results — so it has exactly what it needs and nothing that distracts it.
concepts.analogy: Prepping a chef’s station before service: the right ingredients within reach, the clutter cleared away.
concepts.example: An agent that pulls only the three relevant files into the prompt, instead of dumping your whole repo, is doing context engineering.

related.text: The grown-up successor to prompt engineering — less about wording, more about what information is present.
Exists to spend the context window wisely.
What long-term memory feeds into.

concepts.deeper: The reframing is that a model is only as good as the context it’s given, so the real work is assembling that context on the fly: system instructions, retrieved documents, session history, and prior tool results — packed to fit the window and ordered so the important parts land where the model attends best. Get this right and mediocre prompts still work; get it wrong and no clever wording saves you.

concepts.oneLiner: The control loop that runs an agent — it decides when to think, which tool to call, and what to do with the result, over and over until the job is done.
concepts.analogy: The conductor of an orchestra: not playing an instrument, but cueing each one at the right moment.
concepts.example: When an agent checks the order database, then calls the shipping API, then writes the reply, the orchestration layer is what sequences those steps.

related.text: The “nervous system” that drives an agent between model and tools.
Runs reasoning patterns like ReAct.
Manages what goes into the context window each turn.

concepts.deeper: It’s the state machine around the “think, act, observe” loop: the model proposes an action, the layer runs the tool, feeds the observation back, and reprompts — repeating until a stop condition. Most agent failures are really orchestration failures: it loops forever, repeats itself, or wanders off the goal. This is also where memory, planning, and guardrails get wired in.

concepts.oneLiner: Giving the model a set of actions it can trigger — search, send an email, run code — so it can do things instead of only talking about them.
concepts.analogy: Handing a brilliant advisor a phone and a keyboard — now the advice becomes action.
concepts.example: The model outputs “call get_weather(‘Paris’)”, your code runs it, and the result comes back for the model to use. That round trip is tool use.

related.text: The “hands” that make an agent more than a chatbot.
Standardized across apps by MCP.
Reading from documents is one kind of tool — see grounding.

concepts.deeper: The model doesn’t run anything itself — it emits a structured request (a function name and arguments matching a schema), your system executes it, and the result is fed back into the context. Reliability hinges on clear tool descriptions and tight schemas: vague or overlapping tools are the top reason a model picks the wrong one or fills in bad arguments.

concepts.oneLiner: A standard that lets separate agents discover each other and work together, instead of everyone wiring up custom connections.
concepts.analogy: A business-card exchange for bots — each agent advertises what it can do and how to reach it.
concepts.example: A “project manager” agent hands a research task to a specialist research agent it found via A2A, then waits for the result.

related.text: The agent-to-agent counterpart to MCP, which connects agents to tools.
What makes multi-agent systems practical.

concepts.deeper: Each agent publishes an “Agent Card” — a JSON file listing its capabilities, endpoint, and auth requirements — so others can discover and call it. Interactions are framed as asynchronous tasks with streaming updates, not simple request-response. Where MCP standardizes an agent reaching for a tool, A2A standardizes one agent delegating to another.

concepts.oneLiner: Using one AI model to score another’s output against a rubric, because “right or wrong” is too crude for judging language.
concepts.analogy: A grading TA — not the professor, but consistent, tireless, and good enough to flag the essays worth a closer look.
concepts.example: After a prompt change, a judge model rates 500 answers for accuracy and tone, so the team sees if quality moved before shipping.

related.text: The automated grader that powers most evals.
Still needs a human in the loop to trust its calls.
A common way to catch a hallucination at scale.

concepts.deeper: You give a capable model a rubric — was it factually grounded, did it follow instructions, was the tone right — and have it score outputs against a golden dataset. It scales judgment that would take humans forever, but it inherits the judge model’s own biases and blind spots, so results should be spot-checked by a domain expert before you trust them.

concepts.oneLiner: Making the model answer from real, retrieved facts instead of its own memory — so it can cite a source instead of guessing.
concepts.analogy: Showing your work with references, rather than answering a pop quiz from memory.
concepts.example: A support bot that pulls the actual refund policy and quotes it — rather than inventing one — is grounded.

related.text: RAG is the most common way to ground an agent.
The main defense against hallucination.
Achieved by giving the agent retrieval tools.

concepts.deeper: Grounding means tying a response to authoritative external data — company docs, a database, live search — fetched at answer time and placed in the context. It sharply reduces made-up facts and makes answers checkable, but it’s only as good as the retrieval: if the wrong documents come back, the model grounds itself in the wrong thing, confidently.

concepts.oneLiner: Splitting a big job across several specialized agents that work together, instead of asking one agent to do everything.
concepts.analogy: A film crew instead of a one-man band — a director, a researcher, a writer, each good at their part.
concepts.example: A “manager” agent hands research to one agent, drafting to another, and formatting to a third, then assembles the pieces.

related.text: Agents that treat other agents as tools.
Held together by protocols like A2A.
Coordinating them is an orchestration problem.

concepts.deeper: The idea mirrors a human org: break a complex process into sub-tasks and give each to a focused agent that’s simpler to build, test, and trust. Common patterns include a coordinator that routes work to specialists, a sequential “assembly line,” and a generator-critic pair for quality. The cost is coordination overhead — more moving parts, more ways for the handoffs to go wrong.

concepts.oneLiner: The practice of testing, monitoring, and improving agents in production — DevOps adapted for software that behaves differently every run.
concepts.analogy: Running a kitchen after opening night: tasting dishes, watching tickets, fixing the recipe while service continues.
concepts.example: Logging every agent run, scoring a sample nightly, and turning each bug report into a permanent test is Agent Ops in action.

related.text: Built on a foundation of evals.
Depends on observability to see what the agent did.
Feeds human feedback back into the loop.

concepts.deeper: Because agent output is probabilistic, you can’t assert output == expected; Agent Ops replaces that with continuous evaluation, tracing, and metrics-driven go/no-go decisions. The loop it closes: capture a real-world failure, reproduce it, convert it into a permanent eval, and re-test forever. It’s a natural evolution of DevOps and MLOps for non-deterministic systems.

concepts.oneLiner: Hard limits placed around an agent so it physically can’t do the dangerous thing, no matter what the model decides.
concepts.analogy: The bumpers in a bowling lane — the ball can wander, but it can’t end up in the gutter.
concepts.example: A rule that blocks any purchase over $100 without human sign-off holds even if a prompt tricks the model into trying.

related.text: The deterministic backstop against prompt injection.
Often implemented as a human-in-the-loop checkpoint.
A leash on what an agent can do.

concepts.deeper: The key move is defense in depth: hardcoded rules outside the model (spending caps, blocked actions, required confirmations) that can’t be reasoned away, plus AI-based “guard models” that screen inputs and outputs for injections or unsafe plans. You never rely on the model’s judgment alone, because that judgment can be manipulated — the code-level limits are what stay predictable and auditable.

concepts.oneLiner: A step-by-step recording of everything an agent did — its reasoning, tool calls, and results — so you can answer “why did it do that?”
concepts.analogy: A flight recorder for your agent — when something goes wrong, you can replay the whole trajectory.
concepts.example: A trace shows the agent picked the wrong tool at step three with a bad argument — now you know exactly what to fix.

related.text: The foundation Agent Ops is built on.
Turns a fuzzy failure into a fixable step you can add to your evals.
How you debug the agent, not just the model.

concepts.deeper: It rests on three pillars: logs (what happened), traces (the full ordered path of a single run, with each prompt, tool, parameter, and observation), and metrics (aggregate health like latency, cost, and quality scores). You can’t set a breakpoint inside a model’s “thought,” so the trace is how you see the reasoning trajectory and find the root cause. Standards like OpenTelemetry make this portable.

concepts.oneLiner: How an agent holds on to information — the running scratchpad of the current task, plus a longer store it can recall across sessions.
concepts.analogy: A desk notepad for today’s work, and a filing cabinet for everything worth keeping.
concepts.example: An assistant that remembers next week you prefer aisle seats — without being told again — is using long-term memory.

related.text: What context engineering pulls from each turn.
Long-term memory is usually a RAG system under the hood.
Lives inside the context window while active.

concepts.deeper: Short-term memory is the session scratchpad — the running history of actions and observations the model needs to decide its next step. Long-term memory persists across sessions and is almost always implemented as a separate tool: a vector store the agent writes to and later retrieves from. The hard parts are deciding what’s worth remembering, and pulling the right memory back into context at the right moment.

concepts.oneLiner: A loop where the model reasons about what to do, takes one action, sees the result, then reasons again — the basic rhythm of most agents.
concepts.analogy: Cooking from a recipe you’re also writing: taste, adjust, take the next step, taste again.
concepts.example: “I need the roster, so I’ll call get_team_roster” → runs it → “now I have five names, next I’ll check their calendars.” That’s ReAct.

related.text: The reasoning pattern the orchestration layer runs.
A cousin of chain of thought, but with actions between the thoughts.
The loop that defines how an agent works.

concepts.deeper: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with tool actions: think, act, observe, repeat — instead of reasoning all the way to an answer in one shot. Letting the model see each observation before planning the next step makes it far better at multi-step tasks and grounds its reasoning in real results. It’s the pattern under most agent frameworks, even when they dress it up.

concepts.oneLiner: An agent that operates a screen the way a person would — clicking buttons, filling forms, navigating pages — instead of calling a clean API.
concepts.analogy: Handing the AI a mouse and keyboard and letting it drive, rather than plugging it into the wiring directly.
concepts.example: When there’s no API, an agent can open the web page, click through the booking form, and submit it — that’s computer use.

related.text: A kind of tool an agent can wield.
Risky enough that it usually keeps a human in the loop.
A wide-open door for prompt injection from what’s on screen.

concepts.deeper: The agent takes screenshots, decides where to click or type, and acts on the raw interface — reaching systems that never exposed an API. It’s powerful and general but slower, more brittle, and less safe than a proper tool: a stray button or a malicious instruction hidden on a page can derail it, which is why oversight and confirmation steps matter here more than anywhere.

concepts.oneLiner: Giving each agent its own verifiable ID — separate from the user and the developer — so its actions can be permissioned and audited.
concepts.analogy: An employee badge for a bot: it says who this agent is and exactly which doors it may open.
concepts.example: A sales agent gets read/write to the CRM but is flatly denied HR data — because its identity carries its own permissions.

related.text: The basis for putting guardrails on what an agent can touch.
Essential once agents act on your behalf.
Contains the blast radius if an agent is hijacked by prompt injection.

concepts.deeper: Traditional security knows two kinds of actor: human users and service accounts. Agents are a third — autonomous, acting with delegated authority — so they need their own cryptographic identity (via standards like SPIFFE) rather than borrowing a human’s. With a real identity, an agent gets least-privilege permissions and every action traces back to it, so a compromised agent can only reach the little it was granted.

concepts.oneLiner: A database that stores text as coordinates and finds things by meaning, not keywords — the memory bank behind search that “just gets it.”
concepts.analogy: A library organized by what books are about, not by title — ask for something and the neighbors are all related.
concepts.example: Search “how do I cancel” and it surfaces the “ending your subscription” doc, because their vectors sit close together.

related.text: Stores the embeddings that make it work.
The retrieval engine underneath RAG.
Where an agent’s long-term memory usually lives.

concepts.deeper: Text is turned into embeddings — long lists of numbers — and the database indexes them so it can quickly find the nearest vectors to a query (approximate nearest-neighbor search). “Near” means similar in meaning. It’s the storage layer that makes semantic search, RAG, and long-term memory fast enough to use at scale, even over millions of chunks.

concepts.oneLiner: Emerging standards that let an agent pay or transact on your behalf — with proof you actually authorized it.
concepts.analogy: A signed permission slip for a bot: it can spend, but only within what you clearly agreed to.
concepts.example: You tell an agent “book the flight under $400” and it pays — backed by a signed mandate proving those were your terms.

related.text: Builds on the agent-to-agent protocol.
A big reason to keep a human in the loop on real money.
Raises the stakes of prompt injection enormously.

concepts.deeper: The web assumes a human clicks “buy,” so an autonomous agent spending money creates a trust gap — who’s accountable if it goes wrong? Two protocols are early answers: AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) uses cryptographically-signed “mandates” as verifiable proof of user intent, and x402 uses the HTTP 402 “Payment Required” code for tiny machine-to-machine payments. Both are early and unsettled, but they aim to be the trust layer for an agent economy.

concepts.oneLiner: Models that think before they answer — spending extra compute working through a problem internally instead of blurting the first response.
concepts.analogy: The colleague who pauses and works it out on scratch paper, versus the one who answers instantly and is sometimes wrong.
concepts.example: Give a hard logic puzzle to a reasoning model and it quietly works through steps first, landing the answer far more often.

related.text: Chain of thought, now baked in and hidden instead of prompted.
They trade latency and tokens for accuracy.
The stronger “brain” behind capable agents.

concepts.deeper: They internalize chain-of-thought: instead of you prompting “think step by step,” the model does it by default, spending more compute (and tokens) on a hidden scratchpad before replying. That buys big gains on math, code, and multi-step logic, at the cost of speed and price. The reasoning is often no longer shown to you — same idea as before, just more of it and tucked away.

concepts.oneLiner: The full step-by-step path an agent took to reach an answer — every thought, tool call, and result along the way.
concepts.analogy: Not just the destination, but the whole GPS route — where it turned, backtracked, and why.
concepts.example: Two agents give the same right answer, but one took twelve messy steps and the other took three — the trajectory tells them apart.

related.text: What a trace records so you can inspect it.
Judging the path, not just the output, is a core eval move.
Produced by the think-act-observe loop.

concepts.deeper: For agents, the final answer isn’t enough — a right answer reached by a lucky, wasteful, or unsafe path is still a problem. Trajectory evaluation (“the glass box”) judges the whole sequence of decisions: did it pick the right tools, in a sensible order, without needless steps? It’s how you catch quality and safety issues that a correct-looking output would hide.

concepts.oneLiner: AI that makes new things — text, images, music, code — instead of just sorting or labeling what already exists.
concepts.analogy: The difference between a critic who rates paintings and an artist who paints new ones.
concepts.example: Ask a tool to write a poem or draw a cat surfing and get something that never existed before — that’s generative AI.

related.text: Almost always a deep learning model under the hood.
For text, it usually means a large language model.
The early image version was built on GANs.

concepts.deeper: It learns the patterns in a huge pile of examples, then samples from those patterns to produce something new rather than retrieving a stored answer. The same core idea powers chatbots, image generators, and code assistants — only the training data and output format change.

concepts.oneLiner: Software that learns patterns from examples instead of being programmed with explicit rules.
concepts.analogy: Teaching by showing thousands of examples rather than writing out every rule by hand.
concepts.example: A spam filter that improves from the messages you mark as junk is machine learning, not hand-coded rules.

related.text: Deep learning is the branch that powers modern AI.
The umbrella that neural networks live under.
Its most common flavor is supervised learning.

concepts.deeper: Instead of a human writing “if X then Y” rules, the system adjusts its own internal numbers until its predictions match the examples. Most of what people call “AI” today is machine learning — the older rule-based approach is a separate, much smaller world.

concepts.oneLiner: Machine learning that stacks many layers of neural network — the approach that made modern AI actually work.
concepts.analogy: An assembly line where each station spots slightly bigger patterns — edges, then shapes, then faces.
concepts.example: Face unlock, voice assistants, and ChatGPT are all deep learning under different coats of paint.

related.text: It’s machine learning done with big neural networks.
The transformer is the deep-learning design behind today’s chatbots.
“Deep” means many layers trained by backpropagation.

concepts.deeper: “Deep” just means many layers stacked between input and output. More layers let the model learn richer, more abstract patterns, but need far more data and compute — which is why deep learning only took off once GPUs and huge datasets arrived.

concepts.oneLiner: The web of simple math units, loosely inspired by brain cells, that most AI models are built from.
concepts.analogy: A huge dimmer-switch panel — the model learns by nudging millions of dials until the output looks right.
concepts.example: When an app recognizes your dog in a photo, a neural network is doing the seeing.

related.text: Stacked many layers deep, it becomes deep learning.
The dials it tunes are its parameters.
It learns by backpropagation.

concepts.deeper: Each unit takes numbers in, weighs them, and passes a result to the next layer. The “weights” are the dials; training adjusts them so the whole network maps inputs to the right outputs. The brain analogy is loose — it’s really just layered arithmetic at massive scale.

concepts.oneLiner: The instruction you type to an AI — the request it turns into an answer.
concepts.analogy: The order you give a very literal assistant: word it well and you get what you wanted.
concepts.example: “Write a birthday message for my dad who loves fishing” is a prompt.

related.text: Wording prompts well is prompt engineering.
The prompt plus everything around it fills the context window.
A hostile prompt hidden in data is prompt injection.

concepts.deeper: Everything you send the model — question, instructions, examples, pasted documents — is the prompt. The model doesn’t “understand” it so much as continue it: it predicts the most likely response given those words, which is why small wording changes can swing the output.

concepts.oneLiner: An AI trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word — which turns out to be enough to write, summarize, and answer.
concepts.analogy: Autocomplete that read most of the internet and got unnervingly good at it.
concepts.example: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all large language models with a chat wrapper on top.

related.text: Built on the transformer architecture.
GPT is one well-known family of LLMs.
Its confident wrong guesses are hallucinations.

concepts.deeper: It’s a giant neural network trained to guess the next chunk of text, over and over, across trillions of words. That single objective — predict what comes next — is enough to pick up grammar, facts, tone, and reasoning patterns. It generates one token at a time.

concepts.oneLiner: The 2017 neural-network design that made today’s language models possible, by letting a model weigh every word against every other at once.
concepts.analogy: Instead of reading strictly left to right, it reads the whole sentence at once and decides which words matter most to each other.
concepts.example: The “T” in GPT stands for Transformer — it’s the engine under almost every modern AI model.

related.text: The architecture behind every large language model.
Its “attention” trick is what fills the context window.
GPT is a transformer trained to generate text.

concepts.deeper: Its key idea is “attention”: for each word, the model computes how much every other word should influence it, in parallel rather than in sequence. That parallelism is what let training scale to internet-sized data — the leap that took AI from clumsy to fluent.

concepts.oneLiner: The family of OpenAI language models — the “GPT” in ChatGPT — that pushed AI text into the mainstream.
concepts.analogy: A model lineage, like car generations: GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, each bigger and sharper than the last.
concepts.example: GPT-4 can draft an email, explain code, and pass exams that stumped GPT-2 a few years earlier.

related.text: GPT is one family of large language models.
The “T” is for transformer.
ChatGPT is the chat app built on GPT.

concepts.deeper: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer: pre-trained on huge text, transformer-based, generative. Each generation roughly scales up data and parameters, which reliably buys broader knowledge and better reasoning — the trend that “scaling” bets on.

concepts.oneLiner: OpenAI’s chatbot — the app that put large language models in front of everyone in late 2022.
concepts.analogy: The friendly front door to a GPT model: you type, it chats back.
concepts.example: Asking ChatGPT to summarize your notes or plan a trip is using an LLM without ever seeing the machinery.

related.text: It’s a chat wrapper over a GPT model.
Which is a large language model.
Human feedback (RLHF) is what made it feel cooperative.

concepts.deeper: ChatGPT is the product; GPT is the model inside. Its breakthrough wasn’t just the model but the chat format plus tuning with human feedback that made it follow instructions and feel conversational — which is why it, not GPT-3, went viral.

concepts.oneLiner: An older image-generating design where two networks compete — one fakes, one detects — until the fakes look real.
concepts.analogy: A forger and a detective locked in a race: each one gets sharper by trying to beat the other.
concepts.example: The uncanny “this person does not exist” face generators were powered by GANs.

related.text: Largely overtaken by diffusion models for image generation.
An early form of generative AI.
Both sides are neural networks.

concepts.deeper: Introduced in 2014, GANs dominated AI image generation for years: a generator makes fakes, a discriminator judges them, and their tug-of-war improves both. They’re now mostly historical for new tools — diffusion proved easier to train and scale — but GANs are why “generative” entered the conversation.

concepts.oneLiner: The technique behind most modern AI image tools — it learns to turn random noise into a picture, step by step.
concepts.analogy: Sculpting in reverse: start with TV static and gradually clean it into the image you asked for.
concepts.example: Midjourney, DALL·E, and Stable Diffusion all generate images with diffusion.

related.text: It replaced GANs as the go-to for image generation.
Powers text-to-image tools.
A form of generative AI for pictures.

concepts.deeper: Training teaches the model to remove noise from images a little at a time. To generate, it starts from pure noise and repeatedly denoises, guided by your text prompt, until a coherent image emerges. It’s more stable to train than GANs, which is why it took over.

concepts.oneLiner: OpenAI’s image generator — type a description, get a picture.
concepts.analogy: An illustrator that never sleeps and takes any brief, however weird.
concepts.example: “A cat surfing a taco in watercolor” typed into DALL·E returns exactly that.

related.text: Generates images using diffusion.
A text-to-image tool.
The image-side sibling of ChatGPT.

concepts.deeper: DALL·E popularized text-to-image for the public. Under the hood it pairs an understanding of your prompt with a diffusion image generator. The name is a nod to the artist Dalí and the robot WALL·E.

concepts.oneLiner: AI that turns a written description into a picture.
concepts.analogy: Commissioning art by describing it in words instead of picking up a brush.
concepts.example: Typing “a cozy cabin in the snow at dusk” and getting a finished illustration is text-to-image.

related.text: Most tools generate the image with diffusion.
DALL·E is a well-known example.
The visual branch of generative AI.

concepts.deeper: The model links the meaning of your words to visual patterns learned from millions of caption–image pairs, then generates a matching picture. Quality hinges on the prompt and the training data — which is also where copyright and bias questions get sharp.

concepts.oneLiner: The millions or billions of internal numbers a model tunes during training — roughly, its stored knowledge.
concepts.analogy: The dials on that giant dimmer panel; “175 billion parameters” means 175 billion dials.
concepts.example: When people say a model is “bigger,” they usually mean it has more parameters.

related.text: They live inside the neural network.
Setting them is what training does.
Fine-tuning nudges a subset of them.

concepts.deeper: Each parameter is a number the model adjusts to reduce its errors during training. More parameters give more capacity to store patterns, which is why counts ballooned into the billions — though size isn’t everything; data quality and training method matter just as much.

concepts.oneLiner: The pile of examples a model learns from — its entire education, for better and worse.
concepts.analogy: The books, images, and notes you’d hand a student before an exam; whatever’s missing, they won’t know.
concepts.example: A model trained mostly on English text will be shakier in Swahili — the training data shaped it.

related.text: Learning from it sets the model’s parameters.
Its gaps and slants drive hallucinations.
The learning step itself is machine learning.

concepts.deeper: Models don’t memorize their training data so much as absorb its patterns — but its blind spots, biases, and errors get absorbed too. This is why “what was it trained on?” is often the most important question about any AI, and why data quality beats raw quantity.

concepts.oneLiner: The model actually running — doing the work of answering, as opposed to being trained.
concepts.analogy: Training is studying for the test; inference is sitting the exam.
concepts.example: Every time you send a chatbot a message, you’re paying for a moment of inference.

related.text: The opposite phase from training.
Its speed and cost are counted in tokens.
Reasoning models spend more compute here for better answers.

concepts.deeper: A model’s life has two phases: training (expensive, done once, sets the parameters) and inference (cheap per run, done constantly, generates outputs). Most of a deployed model’s ongoing cost is inference, which is why speeding it up is a whole industry.

concepts.oneLiner: Teaching a model with labeled examples — each input paired with the right answer.
concepts.analogy: Flashcards with the answer on the back; the model checks itself against the label.
concepts.example: Show a model thousands of emails tagged “spam” or “not spam” and it learns to sort new ones.

related.text: The most common form of machine learning.
Contrast with unsupervised learning, which has no labels.
Labels are part of the training data.

concepts.deeper: The model makes a guess, compares it to the known label, and adjusts to close the gap — repeated across the dataset. It’s powerful but needs labeled data, which is often expensive to produce; that cost is why other approaches exist.

concepts.oneLiner: Letting a model find patterns in data on its own, with no answer key.
concepts.analogy: Handing someone a box of mixed photos and asking them to sort into groups — without telling them the categories.
concepts.example: Grouping customers into “types” nobody defined in advance is unsupervised learning.

related.text: Contrast with supervised learning, which uses labels.
Language models pre-train this way on raw text.
Embeddings often come out of it.

concepts.deeper: With no labels to match, the model organizes data by similarity and structure alone — clustering, compressing, or predicting missing pieces. Modern LLMs lean on a version of this: predicting the next word in raw text is a self-labeling task that needs no human annotation.

concepts.oneLiner: Training by trial and error, with rewards for good moves and penalties for bad ones.
concepts.analogy: Training a dog with treats — the model repeats what gets rewarded.
concepts.example: AIs that master chess or Go by playing millions of games against themselves use reinforcement learning.

related.text: Tuning chatbots with human ratings is RLHF.
A third path beside supervised and unsupervised learning.
Used to train agents that take actions.

concepts.deeper: The model acts, gets a reward signal, and adjusts to earn more reward over time — no labeled answers required, just a goal to optimize. It shines where “correct” is hard to label but easy to score, like games, robotics, and, increasingly, aligning language models.

concepts.oneLiner: Polishing a raw language model with human ratings so it becomes helpful, honest, and easy to talk to.
concepts.analogy: After the model learns to talk, people grade its answers and it learns to prefer the ones humans liked.
concepts.example: RLHF is a big reason ChatGPT feels cooperative instead of just autocompleting your sentence.

related.text: A form of reinforcement learning.
Applied on top of a pre-trained model.
What turned GPT into ChatGPT.

concepts.deeper: Humans rank competing model answers; those rankings train a “reward model,” which then guides the language model to produce more of what people prefer. It’s the step that aligns a knowledgeable-but-unruly base model with what users actually want — and where much of the “personality” gets set.

concepts.oneLiner: When a model memorizes its training examples instead of learning the general pattern — acing practice, flunking real life.
concepts.analogy: A student who memorized the practice test word-for-word and freezes when the real questions differ.
concepts.example: A model that’s perfect on training data but wrong on anything new has overfit.

related.text: Caught by testing on held-out data during evals.
A risk baked into the training-data step.
More parameters can worsen it without enough data.

concepts.deeper: Overfitting means the model latched onto noise and quirks specific to the training set rather than the underlying pattern. You detect it by checking performance on data the model never saw; the gap between training and test accuracy is the tell.

concepts.oneLiner: The core algorithm that lets a neural network learn — it traces each mistake backward and nudges every dial to do better.
concepts.analogy: After a wrong answer, walking back through the chain to assign a little blame to each step, then correcting each one.
concepts.example: Every time a deep learning model improves during training, backpropagation is doing the adjusting.

related.text: The learning engine inside a neural network.
What it tunes are the parameters.
Repeated over the training data.

concepts.deeper: It works out how much each parameter contributed to the error, then shifts each one slightly to reduce it — repeated millions of times. Conceptually simple and decades old, it’s the quiet workhorse that makes training deep networks possible at all.

concepts.oneLiner: The first, huge phase of learning where a model reads mountains of raw data to build general knowledge — before any fine-tuning.
concepts.analogy: A broad general education, before specializing in a job.
concepts.example: The “P” in GPT is pre-trained: it read much of the internet before it was ever tuned to chat.

related.text: Specializing afterward is fine-tuning.
Aligning it with human ratings is RLHF.
Usually done unsupervised on raw text.

concepts.deeper: Pretraining is where the expensive, general learning happens — predicting the next token across trillions of words builds broad competence. Later, cheaper steps (fine-tuning, RLHF) specialize and align that base. This “pretrain then adapt” recipe is the backbone of modern AI.

concepts.oneLiner: A big, general model trained once on broad data, then adapted for many different tasks.
concepts.analogy: A versatile base ingredient — like flour — that lots of specific dishes get built from.
concepts.example: GPT-4 is a foundation model: the same base powers chat, coding help, and dozens of apps.

related.text: For text, it’s usually a large language model.
Adapting one to your task is fine-tuning.
Its broad skills come from pretraining.

concepts.deeper: The term captures a shift: instead of training a fresh model per task, you build one large, general model and adapt it many ways. That reuse is why a handful of expensive foundation models now sit under thousands of products.

concepts.oneLiner: AI that handles more than one kind of input or output — text, images, audio, video — in a single model.
concepts.analogy: A worker who can read, look at pictures, and listen, instead of only reading.
concepts.example: Snap a photo of your fridge and ask "what can I cook?" — a multimodal model reads the image and replies in text.

related.text: Extends a large language model beyond text.
Text-to-image is one multimodal pairing.
Lets agents use screenshots for computer use.

concepts.deeper: A multimodal model maps different data types into a shared representation so it can reason across them — describe an image, answer questions about a chart, or caption a video. It's where the frontier models are heading, since most real tasks mix formats.

concepts.oneLiner: The hidden instructions loaded before your message that tell the model who it is, what rules to follow, and how to behave.
concepts.analogy: The employee handbook a new hire reads before their first day — the user never sees it, but it shapes everything.
concepts.example: A support bot's system prompt says "you are a helpful assistant for Acme Corp; never discuss competitors" — and it obeys.

related.text: The highest-priority part of the context window.
Designing them well is context engineering.
Can be overridden by prompt injection if unprotected.

concepts.deeper: It sits at the top of the context and carries the most weight in the model's attention. Everything from persona to output format to safety rules goes here. The model treats it as ground truth, which is why getting it right matters more than clever user prompts — and why attackers try to override it.

concepts.oneLiner: The trick that lets a model weigh how much each word matters to every other word — the engine inside every transformer.
concepts.analogy: Reading a sentence and mentally highlighting which words are most connected to each other.
concepts.example: In "The cat sat on the mat because it was tired," attention links "it" back to "cat," not "mat."

related.text: The core innovation of the transformer.
Scales with the context window — longer contexts need more attention compute.

concepts.deeper: For each token, the model computes a score against every other token to decide how much influence each should have. "Multi-head" attention runs several of these in parallel, each learning different relationships (syntax, meaning, coreference). It's what made transformers work — and what makes long context windows expensive.

concepts.oneLiner: A model architecture that routes each input to a few specialist sub-networks instead of using the whole model every time — big capacity, smaller cost.
concepts.analogy: A hospital with many specialists on staff, but each patient only sees the two or three they need.
concepts.example: Mixtral and GPT-4 use MoE — trillions of total parameters, but only a fraction activate per token.

related.text: A way to scale models without scaling inference cost linearly.
Still a transformer under the hood.
Keeps inference cost manageable.

concepts.deeper: A router network decides which "expert" sub-networks handle each token. The model can have enormous total parameters (knowledge capacity) while only running a small subset per forward pass (cost). The tradeoff: training is harder, and load-balancing across experts is its own research problem.

concepts.oneLiner: A shortcut for fine-tuning that trains only a small add-on layer instead of rewriting the whole model — 90% cheaper, nearly as good.
concepts.analogy: Instead of repainting the whole house, you hang new curtains — same impact where it matters, fraction of the effort.
concepts.example: Fine-tune a 70B model to write in your brand voice on a single GPU by training a LoRA adapter that's 0.1% the size.

related.text: The efficient way to do fine-tuning.
QLoRA adds quantization on top, shrinking memory further.
An alternative to just improving your prompts.

concepts.deeper: LoRA freezes all original weights and inserts tiny trainable matrices into the attention layers. Only those matrices update, slashing GPU memory and training time. QLoRA goes further by quantizing the frozen weights to 4-bit first. The adapter can be swapped in and out, so one base model can serve many fine-tuned variants.

concepts.oneLiner: Shrinking a model by using lower-precision numbers — trades a tiny bit of quality for dramatically less memory and faster speed.
concepts.analogy: Switching from high-res photos to slightly compressed ones — barely noticeable, but they take up way less space.
concepts.example: A 70B model that needs 140 GB in full precision fits in 35 GB at 4-bit quantization — suddenly runnable on a gaming PC.

related.text: Often paired with LoRA for efficient fine-tuning (QLoRA).
Reduces the memory footprint of parameters.
What makes local inference on consumer hardware possible.

concepts.deeper: Model weights are stored as numbers. Full precision uses 16 bits per weight; quantization drops that to 8, 4, or even 2 bits. The quality hit is surprisingly small for well-calibrated methods — most users can't tell the difference at 4-bit. GGUF is a popular file format for quantized models in the local-AI ecosystem.

concepts.oneLiner: Training a small model to mimic a large one — keeping most of the smarts at a fraction of the size and cost.
concepts.analogy: A senior mentor training a junior to handle 90% of cases, so the senior only gets called for the hard ones.
concepts.example: A company runs GPT-4 on hard questions but routes easy ones to a distilled model that costs 1/50th as much.

related.text: A way to compress a foundation model for production.
Works alongside quantization for smaller deployments.
The teacher model generates synthetic training data.

concepts.deeper: The "teacher" model generates outputs (including soft probability distributions, not just hard answers) and the smaller "student" model learns to reproduce them. The student ends up far better than if trained from scratch on the same data, because it learns the teacher's reasoning patterns, not just facts.

concepts.oneLiner: Showing the model a handful of examples in the prompt so it picks up the pattern — no training required.
concepts.analogy: Showing someone three completed forms so they know how to fill out the fourth.
concepts.example: Paste five customer emails with their sentiment labels, then paste a sixth without a label — the model labels it correctly.

related.text: Zero-shot means no examples at all.
A core prompt engineering technique.
The examples live inside the context window.

concepts.deeper: The model doesn't learn new weights — it pattern-matches the examples you provided in-context. "One-shot" means one example, "few-shot" means a handful. It's remarkably effective because large models are strong in-context learners, but it eats into your context window, so you balance example count against available space.

concepts.oneLiner: Asking the model to do something it was never specifically shown how to do — no examples, just the instruction.
concepts.analogy: Handing someone a task with no sample and saying "figure it out" — and they do.
concepts.example: "Classify this review as positive or negative" with no examples — the model just knows how.

related.text: Add a few examples and it becomes few-shot.
Works because pre-training gave the model broad knowledge.

concepts.deeper: Zero-shot ability is what makes large language models feel magical — they generalize from pretraining alone, without task-specific examples. It works best for tasks close to what the model saw during training and degrades for unusual or highly specialized ones, where few-shot examples dramatically help.

concepts.oneLiner: The model picking up a new skill on the fly from whatever you put in the prompt — without any retraining.
concepts.analogy: A quick learner who adapts to a new task just by reading the brief, without going back to school.
concepts.example: Give it a few English-to-French translations, then a new English sentence — it translates, even though you never fine-tuned it on French.

related.text: Few-shot learning is the most common form.
Why context engineering matters so much.
Happens inside the context window at inference time.

concepts.deeper: The model adjusts its behavior based on the patterns in its current context — no gradient updates, no parameter changes. This emergent ability is one of the most surprising properties of large models, and it's why prompt design has such outsized impact. The mechanism isn't fully understood, but it appears to work like implicit Bayesian inference over the examples provided.

concepts.oneLiner: Splitting documents into smaller pieces before feeding them to a retrieval system — the unglamorous step that makes or breaks RAG.
concepts.analogy: Cutting a textbook into flash cards — too big and you get noise, too small and you lose context.
concepts.example: A 50-page manual gets split into 500-word sections, each embedded separately, so search can retrieve just the relevant part.

related.text: The critical prep step for RAG.
Each chunk becomes an embedding in a vector database.
Bad chunking is usually why retrieval returns irrelevant results.

concepts.deeper: Strategies range from simple (split every N tokens) to smart (split at paragraph or section boundaries, overlap chunks so context isn't lost at edges). Semantic chunking uses a model to detect topic shifts. Chunk size is the biggest knob: too large and retrieval returns noise alongside the answer; too small and the chunk lacks enough context to be useful on its own.

concepts.oneLiner: Search that matches by meaning, not keywords — type "how to cancel" and find the doc titled "ending your subscription."
concepts.analogy: A librarian who understands what you're looking for, not just the exact words you used.
concepts.example: Search your docs for "pricing" and get results about "cost," "rates," and "plans" — because they mean similar things.

related.text: Powered by embeddings under the hood.
Stored and queried in a vector database.
The retrieval mechanism inside RAG.

concepts.deeper: Your query and every document chunk are turned into embedding vectors. The search engine finds documents whose vectors are closest to the query vector (by cosine similarity). It's why AI-powered search "just gets it" compared to keyword search — but it can also match things that are semantically similar but factually wrong, so precision tuning matters.

concepts.oneLiner: The work of making AI systems behave the way humans intend — helpful, honest, and not harmful.
concepts.analogy: Not just teaching someone skills, but making sure they use those skills responsibly.
concepts.example: A model that refuses to help build weapons, admits uncertainty, and follows instructions is "aligned."

related.text: RLHF is the main alignment technique today.
DPO is a simpler alternative.
The broader field this falls under is AI safety.

concepts.deeper: Alignment is the gap between "capable" and "reliably good." A model can be brilliant and still be sycophantic, deceptive, or harmful if alignment fails. Current techniques (RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI) work well enough for today's models, but whether they scale to much more capable systems is an open and high-stakes question.

concepts.oneLiner: A simpler way to align a model with human preferences — skip the reward model, just train directly on which answer people liked better.
concepts.analogy: Instead of hiring a judge to score essays, you just show the student which one the teacher preferred and say "be more like that."
concepts.example: Collect pairs of responses where humans picked a winner, then train the model to favor the winning style — no separate reward model needed.

related.text: The simpler alternative to RLHF.
Both are alignment techniques.
Applied after pretraining.

concepts.deeper: RLHF needs a separate reward model trained on preferences, then uses RL to optimize against it — complex and unstable. DPO collapses this into a single training step by reformulating the preference problem as a classification loss. Simpler, cheaper, and often competitive in quality, which is why it's rapidly replacing RLHF in many pipelines.

concepts.oneLiner: Deliberately trying to break an AI — finding the prompts that make it say or do things it shouldn't.
concepts.analogy: Hiring a burglar to test your locks before a real thief shows up.
concepts.example: A team spends a week trying to get the chatbot to leak its system prompt, produce harmful content, or ignore its guardrails.

related.text: Tests the guardrails.
A form of eval focused on safety.
Tries to exploit prompt injection.

concepts.deeper: Red teamers probe for jailbreaks, harmful outputs, bias, privacy leaks, and edge-case failures — anything the model should refuse but might not. It's both a pre-launch audit and an ongoing practice, because new attack techniques keep emerging. The findings feed directly into better alignment and guardrails.

concepts.oneLiner: Training data generated by AI rather than collected from the real world — faster and cheaper, but watch for feedback loops.
concepts.analogy: A flight simulator instead of real flights — useful for practice, dangerous if you forget it's not the real thing.
concepts.example: Use GPT-4 to generate 10,000 customer-support conversations to train a smaller model, instead of collecting real ones.

related.text: Often used in distillation — the teacher generates it.
Quality still matters just as much as with real training data.
A growing part of alignment pipelines.

concepts.deeper: As real data runs out (or is legally risky), synthetic data fills the gap. The risk is "model collapse" — training on AI-generated data that drifts from reality over generations, amplifying errors and losing diversity. Best practice: mix synthetic with real data and validate quality carefully.

concepts.oneLiner: A standardized test for AI models — a fixed set of questions so you can compare apples to apples.
concepts.analogy: The SAT for AI — not perfect, but everyone takes the same test so scores are comparable.
concepts.example: MMLU tests general knowledge, HumanEval tests coding, and Chatbot Arena lets humans vote — all benchmarks.

related.text: A specific type of eval.
What you check before picking a foundation model.
Models are sometimes tuned to game them, which undermines the point.

concepts.deeper: Popular ones: MMLU (broad knowledge), HumanEval (code), GSM8K (math), LMSYS Chatbot Arena (human preference). The catch is Goodhart's Law — once a benchmark becomes a target, models get optimized for it and scores stop reflecting real capability. The best teams use public benchmarks for rough positioning and internal evals for real decisions.

concepts.oneLiner: Models whose weights are publicly available so anyone can download, run, and modify them — the open-source movement for AI.
concepts.analogy: The difference between renting a car and owning one — you can look under the hood, modify it, and drive it wherever you want.
concepts.example: Meta's Llama and Mistral's models can be downloaded and run on your own servers — no API key or usage fees.

related.text: What you run locally with tools like Ollama.
Often quantized to fit on consumer hardware.
Fine-tuned with LoRA for specific tasks.

concepts.deeper: Strictly, most "open-source" models are open-weight — the weights are shared, but the training data and full recipe often aren't. Still, they've democratized AI: companies that can't send data to external APIs run open-weight models on-premise. The trade-off is capability (frontier closed models still lead) and the responsibility of hosting, safety-filtering, and updating yourself.

concepts.oneLiner: The most popular framework for building LLM-powered apps — it wires together models, tools, memory, and retrieval into working chains.
concepts.analogy: LEGO bricks for AI apps — snap together a retriever, a model, and a formatter and you have a working pipeline.
concepts.example: A RAG chatbot built in LangChain: load docs → chunk → embed → retrieve → prompt the model → return the answer, all in a few lines.

related.text: LangGraph is its agent framework for complex workflows.
Handles the retrieval side of RAG.
An orchestration framework.

concepts.deeper: LangChain provides abstractions for prompts, models, retrievers, tools, and memory, plus pre-built "chains" that compose them. Critics say it over-abstracts simple things, but it's the de facto starting point for most LLM projects. Its ecosystem includes LangSmith (tracing) and LangGraph (agents).

concepts.oneLiner: A framework for building AI agents as graphs — each node is a step, each edge is a decision, and the whole thing runs as a state machine.
concepts.analogy: A flowchart that actually executes — draw the workflow, and the agent follows it.
concepts.example: Build a research agent where one node searches, another summarizes, a third checks quality, and a loop edge sends bad results back for retry.

related.text: Built on top of LangChain.
Implements the orchestration layer as a directed graph.
Supports human-in-the-loop checkpoints natively.

concepts.deeper: LangGraph models agent workflows as directed graphs with typed state. Nodes are functions (model calls, tool invocations, human approvals); edges route based on the current state. This makes complex patterns — branching, looping, parallel execution, human interrupts — explicit and debuggable instead of buried in code. It's LangChain's answer to the "agents need more structure than a simple loop" problem.

concepts.oneLiner: The GitHub of AI — a platform where people share models, datasets, and tools, plus libraries to use them.
concepts.analogy: An app store for AI models: browse, download, and plug in.
concepts.example: Search Hugging Face for "sentiment analysis," find a model, and have it running in three lines of Python.

related.text: Where most open-weight models are published.
Its Transformers library is the standard way to load models.
Hosts datasets for training.

concepts.deeper: Hugging Face hosts over a million models and datasets, plus the Transformers library (the standard Python interface for loading and running models), Datasets, Spaces (hosted demos), and inference APIs. It's become the central hub of the open AI ecosystem — if a model isn't on Hugging Face, it might as well not exist for many developers.

concepts.oneLiner: A tool for running AI models on your own computer — download a model, type one command, and chat locally with no cloud needed.
concepts.analogy: Docker for AI models — pull and run, no cloud required.
concepts.example: Run `ollama run llama3` and you're chatting with a 70B model entirely on your machine, no API key needed.

related.text: Runs open-weight models locally.
Uses quantized models to fit in consumer hardware.
An alternative to cloud API inference.

concepts.deeper: Ollama packages quantized models in an easy-to-use CLI with an OpenAI-compatible API. It abstracts away the complexity of model formats, GPU memory management, and serving. It's become the default way hobbyists and privacy-conscious teams run local models — part of the broader movement away from sending everything to the cloud.

concepts.oneLiner: The finding that making models bigger and feeding them more data predictably makes them smarter — the bet the whole industry is built on.
concepts.analogy: A recipe where doubling the ingredients reliably makes a bigger cake — until you run out of oven space.
concepts.example: GPT-3 to GPT-4 followed scaling laws: more parameters, more data, more compute, better results.

related.text: Drives the growth in parameters.
Why training data is so valuable.
Why pre-training is so expensive.

concepts.deeper: Research (notably from OpenAI and DeepMind's "Chinchilla") showed that model performance scales as a power law with compute, data, and parameters. This predictability is why companies pour billions into training — they can forecast the quality jump before spending. The open question is how long the trend holds before diminishing returns or data scarcity kicks in.

concepts.oneLiner: The field of making sure AI systems don't cause harm — from today's chatbot glitches to tomorrow's autonomous risks.
concepts.analogy: Automotive safety engineering — not just building a fast car, but making sure it has brakes, seatbelts, and crash testing.
concepts.example: Testing a model for bias, building kill switches for agents, and researching alignment are all AI safety work.

related.text: Alignment is the core technical challenge.
Red teaming is how you find the gaps.
Guardrails are the practical safety layer.

concepts.deeper: AI safety spans a spectrum: near-term (bias, toxicity, privacy, misuse) and long-term (loss of control, deceptive alignment, power concentration). The near-term work is engineering — evals, guardrails, audits. The long-term work is more research-flavored and contested, but both share the goal of keeping increasingly capable systems under meaningful human control.

concepts.oneLiner: The open-source image generator that put AI art on everyone's computer — free to download, modify, and run locally.
concepts.analogy: Photoshop meets open source — anyone can use it, modify it, and build on it.
concepts.example: Run Stable Diffusion on your laptop, type "oil painting of a cyberpunk city at sunset," and get a finished image in 30 seconds.

related.text: Built on diffusion models.
The open-weight alternative to DALL·E and Midjourney.
A text-to-image tool.

concepts.deeper: Released by Stability AI in 2022, it was the first high-quality image model with publicly available weights. That openness spawned an enormous ecosystem: custom fine-tunes, ControlNet for precise composition, community model hubs, and local UIs. It's where the open-source image-gen community lives.

concepts.oneLiner: An AI image generator known for stunning, artistic output — runs through Discord, no local setup needed.
concepts.analogy: A commissioned artist in the cloud: describe what you want and get polished results.
concepts.example: Type "/imagine a watercolor fox reading a newspaper" in Discord and Midjourney returns four gorgeous variations.

related.text: Competes with DALL·E and Stable Diffusion.
A text-to-image tool.
Its aesthetic quality set user expectations for AI art.

concepts.deeper: Midjourney carved its niche by prioritizing aesthetic quality over photorealism — its images look like art, not stock photos. It runs entirely as a cloud service (originally Discord-only, now also web), so there's nothing to download or host. The trade-off: it's a closed, paid service with no model weights to download or fine-tune.

concepts.oneLiner: Anthropic's family of AI models — known for strong reasoning, long context windows, and a focus on safety.
concepts.analogy: A colleague who reads the whole document before answering, not just the first page.
concepts.example: Paste a 200-page contract into Claude and ask for a summary of key risks — it handles the full thing.

related.text: A large language model.
Aligned using techniques like RLHF and Constitutional AI.
Competes with GPT and Gemini.

concepts.deeper: Anthropic builds Claude with a focus on safety research and alignment. The model family spans sizes (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) for different cost/capability needs. It's known for strong instruction-following, long context (up to hundreds of thousands of tokens), and agentic tool use via features like computer use and MCP.

concepts.oneLiner: Google's AI model family — natively multimodal, tightly integrated with Google's ecosystem.
concepts.analogy: Google's entry in the AI race — with the advantage of being baked into Search, Docs, and everything else.
concepts.example: Ask Gemini in Google Docs to summarize a spreadsheet and draft an email about it — all without leaving the Google workspace.

related.text: A large language model.
Natively multimodal — text, image, audio, video.
Competes with GPT and Claude.

concepts.deeper: Gemini was built multimodal from the start — not a text model with vision bolted on, but trained across modalities natively. The family spans Flash (fast/cheap), Pro (balanced), and Ultra (frontier). Its biggest edge is integration with Google's products and data, which no other model has.

concepts.oneLiner: The hidden mathematical space where a model stores its understanding — where "similar" things end up near each other.
concepts.analogy: A map the model draws internally — not of places, but of ideas, where related concepts sit close together.
concepts.example: In a diffusion model's latent space, "golden retriever" and "labrador" are neighbors, while "truck" is in a different region entirely.

related.text: Embeddings are coordinates in a latent space.
Diffusion models generate images by navigating it.
What a neural network learns to construct.

concepts.deeper: A model compresses high-dimensional input (text, images) into a lower-dimensional representation where structure emerges — meanings cluster, relationships become geometric. Diffusion models work entirely in latent space (which is why Stable Diffusion is technically a "latent diffusion model"), and LLMs build rich latent representations at every layer. It's the internal world the model reasons over.

concepts.oneLiner: When a model's outputs systematically favor or disfavor certain groups — usually because its training data did.
concepts.analogy: A mirror that doesn't reflect everyone equally — it shows some people clearly and distorts others.
concepts.example: A hiring model trained mostly on male résumés starts ranking women lower — not because it was told to, but because the data leaned that way.

related.text: Rooted in the training data.
Alignment tries to reduce it.
Red teaming is how you find it.

concepts.deeper: Bias enters at every stage: data collection (who's represented), labeling (whose judgments), model design (what's optimized), and deployment (who's affected). It's not just a technical bug — it reflects and can amplify real-world inequities. Mitigations include diverse training data, bias audits, disaggregated evaluation, and ongoing monitoring in production.

concepts.oneLiner: The field of teaching computers to understand, generate, and work with human language — the discipline behind chatbots, translators, and search.
concepts.analogy: Teaching a computer to read and write, not just process data.
concepts.example: Spam filtering, autocomplete, translation, and chatbots are all NLP applications.

related.text: Large language models are the current NLP powerhouse.
The transformer revolutionized the field.
Pre-LLM NLP used techniques like BERT.

concepts.deeper: NLP existed long before ChatGPT — decades of work on parsing, sentiment analysis, machine translation, and named-entity recognition. The transformer/LLM era collapsed many separate NLP tasks into "just prompt the model," but the field's core questions (how to represent meaning, handle ambiguity, evaluate quality) remain as relevant as ever.

concepts.oneLiner: Google's 2018 model that taught the AI world how to understand text by reading in both directions — the bridge between old NLP and the LLM era.
concepts.analogy: The model that made reading comprehension work — not by generating text, but by deeply understanding it.
concepts.example: BERT powered Google Search's ability to understand that "bank" means different things in "river bank" vs. "bank account."

related.text: A transformer, but an encoder (understanding) not a decoder (generating).
Pre-trained then fine-tuned — the pattern LLMs inherited.
Largely replaced by LLMs for new projects.

concepts.deeper: BERT reads text bidirectionally (both left-to-right and right-to-left simultaneously) to build deep understanding. It dominated NLP from 2018–2022 for classification, search ranking, and entity extraction. It's fading as a first choice now — LLMs handle most of its tasks — but BERT-family models (RoBERTa, DistilBERT) still run in production where fast, cheap classification beats calling an LLM.

concepts.oneLiner: An AI that works alongside you in your tools — suggesting code, drafting emails, or filling spreadsheets as you go.
concepts.analogy: A skilled apprentice sitting next to you, handing you the tool you're about to reach for.
concepts.example: GitHub Copilot suggests the next line of code as you type; Microsoft Copilot drafts an email from bullet points in Outlook.

related.text: Powered by large language models under the hood.
The lighter sibling of a full agent — it assists rather than acts.
Evolved from autocomplete into something much smarter.

concepts.deeper: Copilots sit between simple autocomplete and full agents: they suggest, draft, and assist within an existing tool, but the human stays in the driver's seat. The pattern has spread from coding (GitHub Copilot, Cursor) to office suites (Microsoft 365 Copilot) to design tools. The line between "copilot" and "agent" is blurring as these tools gain the ability to take multi-step actions.

concepts.oneLiner: Reusing what a model learned on one task to do well on a different one — the reason you can fine-tune instead of training from scratch.
concepts.analogy: A chef trained in French cuisine picking up Japanese cooking faster than someone starting from zero — the knife skills transfer.
concepts.example: A model trained on millions of web pages transfers that knowledge to your specific customer-support task after a small amount of fine-tuning.

related.text: Fine-tuning is transfer learning in practice.
Foundation models are designed for this.
What pretraining enables.

concepts.deeper: Transfer learning is the insight that made modern AI practical: instead of training from scratch for every task (expensive, needs tons of data), you take a model pretrained on broad data and adapt it cheaply. This is why the pretrain-then-adapt recipe dominates — the broad knowledge transfers, and you only need a little task-specific data to specialize it.

concepts.oneLiner: A library that handles the plumbing of building agents — the loop, tools, memory, and error handling — so you focus on the task, not the wiring.
concepts.analogy: Rails for agent development — it gives you the structure so you're not reinventing the wheel for every agent.
concepts.example: Pick LangGraph, CrewAI, or Anthropic's Agent SDK, define your tools and goals, and the framework handles the orchestration loop.

related.text: LangGraph is a popular choice.
They implement the orchestration layer.
Built to run the ReAct pattern and its variants.

concepts.deeper: Frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and Anthropic's Agent SDK abstract the think-act-observe loop, tool registration, memory management, and error recovery. They differ in philosophy: some are graph-based (LangGraph), some are role-based multi-agent (CrewAI), some minimal (smolagents). Choosing one is mostly about how much control vs. convenience you want and whether your use case is single-agent or multi-agent.

concepts.oneLiner: An alignment approach where the model critiques and revises its own outputs against a set of written principles — less human labeling, more self-improvement.
concepts.analogy: Giving a model a constitution to follow and asking it to check its own work against it.
concepts.example: The model generates an answer, then asks itself "does this violate any of these principles?" and rewrites if so — before the user ever sees it.

related.text: An alternative alignment technique to RLHF.
Developed by Anthropic for Claude.
Part of the broader alignment effort.

concepts.deeper: Developed by Anthropic, CAI reduces dependence on human feedback by having the model self-critique against a set of written principles (the "constitution"). The model generates, critiques, and revises its own outputs, then those improved outputs are used for RL training. It's cheaper and more scalable than pure RLHF, and the principles are transparent and auditable — you can read exactly what rules the model was trained to follow.

concepts.oneLiner: The tool that chops text into tokens before the model sees it — the reason "strawberry" doesn't have three R's according to AI.
concepts.analogy: A paper shredder that cuts text into specific-sized pieces — the model only sees the pieces, never the full page.
concepts.example: "unbelievable" becomes ["un", "believ", "able"] — three tokens. The model never sees individual letters.

related.text: Creates the tokens the model reads.
Why models struggle with character-level tasks like counting letters.
Different models use different tokenizers, which affects multilingual performance.

concepts.deeper: Most modern tokenizers use Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): start with individual bytes, then iteratively merge the most common pairs into larger tokens. Common words become single tokens; rare words get split into pieces. This is why models miscount letters (they literally can't see them), why some languages cost more tokens, and why typos confuse models disproportionately.

concepts.oneLiner: Knobs that control which words the model is allowed to pick from — trimming the unlikely options to keep output focused or creative.
concepts.analogy: Telling a chef "pick from your best five ingredients" (top-k) or "pick from ingredients that together make up 90% of what's good" (top-p).
concepts.example: Top-k=50 means only the 50 most likely next words are considered. Top-p=0.9 means words are considered until their probabilities add up to 90%.

related.text: Works alongside temperature to shape output.
All are sampling knobs applied at inference time.
